range, lifespan, and overall efﬁciency. However, they remain
highly susceptible to issues such as capacity degradation,
thermal instability, and lithium plating, which can compromise
both safety and performance. These challenges highlight the
urgent need for advanced diagnostic frameworks capable of
accurately monitoring battery health and estimating remaining
capacity under diverse and dynamic real-world conditions.
In this work, we distinguish between battery health anomaly

detection and capacity estimation, two related yet distinct
diagnostic tasks. Following established battery diagnostics
conventions [1], State of Health (SoH) refers to the overall
degradation of the battery (often expressed as a percentage
of initial capacity), whereas capacity estimation quantiﬁes the
absolute remaining charge in ampere-hours (Ah). Accordingly,
we frame health monitoring as a binary anomaly detection task
(normal vs. anomalous conditions such as lithium plating or
thermal runaway), and capacity estimation as a regression task.
The complexity of battery diagnostics stems from the highly

variable operating environments of EVs [2], which involve
ﬂuctuating charging and discharging cycles, environmental
conditions, and aging effects. Traditional methods, such as
physics-based models or predeﬁned threshold-based diagnos-
tics, struggle to adapt to such real-world complexities, often
leading to suboptimal performance. Moreover, the integration
of EVs into connected vehicular networks introduces addi-
tional constraints, including the need for scalable solutions that
can handle large data volumes while preserving data privacy.
Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for battery

diagnostics, leveraging multivariate time-series data to identify
anomalies and predict capacity trends [2], [3], [4]. However,
deploying these models in distributed electric vehicle (EV)
ﬂeets presents several critical challenges. EVs, with their
limited processing power and memory, cannot feasibly train or
host complex machine learning models locally. Furthermore,
transferring raw battery data to centralized servers raises
signiﬁcant privacy concerns, particularly within large-scale
vehicular networks. This necessitates solutions that safeguard
sensitive information while enabling effective model train-
ing. The variability in battery usage patterns and operational
conditions across EVs further complicates the creation of
generalized models, as the heterogeneous data demands robust
approaches to maintain predictive accuracy. Additionally, the
exponential growth in the number of EVs calls for scalable
frameworks capable of efﬁciently handling model updates and

2
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON CONSUMER ELECTRONICS

managing communication overhead between EV clients and
parameter servers. To be practical, such solutions must also
align with existing EV infrastructure, exploiting idle periods,
such as charging sessions, for computational tasks without
compromising the energy and operational requirements of the
EVs.
To address these challenges, this paper introduces a Split
Federated Learning framework combined with a multi-task
transformer-based model designed to address two critical
tasks: battery health anomaly detection and capacity esti-
mation. The framework uses a uniﬁed approach, leveraging
a single model for both tasks, which simpliﬁes deployment
and reduces operational complexity. This approach eliminates
the need for training and maintaining separate models for
each task, resulting in signiﬁcant practical and computational
beneﬁts.
The proposed framework employs a hierarchical federated
learning architecture that integrates EVs, edge servers at
charging stations, and a global server in the cloud. By using
federated learning principles, sensitive data remains localized
at the EV level, safeguarding privacy while enabling col-
laborative training across distributed nodes. Furthermore, the
hierarchical design coordinates learning across multiple levels,
ensuring model consistency and scalability. The use of split
learning further enhances the system’s efﬁciency by dividing
the model into segments, with only the initial layers being
trained locally on the EV, while the rest are processed on the
edge server. This design minimizes computational demands on
EVs, making the framework suitable for resource-constrained
devices. Another critical advantage of this approach is the
optimization of training sessions during the EV’s charging
periods. By performing training while the EV is connected
to the charging station, the framework avoids depleting the
battery for computational tasks, preserving energy for essential
functionalities. These design considerations make the proposed
solution practical and efﬁcient, aligning with the energy and
privacy requirements of modern EV systems.
To summarize, the main contributions of this paper are:

• Developing a single model capable of performing both
battery health and capacity estimation. This uniﬁed
approach, facilitated by split learning, simpliﬁes deploy-
ment, reduces complexity, and enhances energy efﬁciency
by allowing EVs to train only a portion of the model
locally while ofﬂoading the remaining computations to
the edge server. This minimizes computational demands
on EVs and ensures scalability for real-world applica-
tions.

• Introducing a privacy-preserving and scalable federated
learning architecture that integrates differential privacy
mechanisms to protect sensitive data. The framework
facilitates seamless collaboration among EVs, edge
servers at charging stations, and a global parameter server,
ensuring efﬁcient training across EVs while maintaining
model consistency and safeguarding sensitive data within
the EVs.

• Demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness of the
proposed solution through rigorous validation on a recent
and realistic, large-scale EV dataset, achieving superior

performance over state-of-the-art methods for both bat-
tery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation
tasks.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section II reviews the related work. Section III details
the development and operation of the proposed framework.
Section IV presents the performance evaluation results along
with a comparative analysis against state-of-the-art (SOTA)
approaches. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

Battery diagnostics and capacity estimation are critical
research areas for ensuring the safety, reliability, and oper-
ational efﬁciency of electric vehicles (EVs). Early approaches
often relied on statistical models and traditional machine
learning techniques, such as statistical distribution analysis
and canonical algorithms, to diagnose faults and detect anoma-
lies [5], [6]. More recently, Li et al. [7] review artiﬁcial neural
network (ANN) approaches for state-of-health (SoH) estima-
tion and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, discussing
battery aging mechanisms, available datasets, and ANN archi-
tectures, and outlining key challenges related to deployment
feasibility and model interpretability.
Sultan et al. [8] propose an active cell balancing system to
address imbalanced state of charge (SoC) in EV lithium-ion
battery packs caused by cell inconsistencies. The study eval-
uates seven machine learning models for predicting battery
lifespan and remaining useful life (RUL). Das et al. [9]
estimate the state of health (SoH) of lithium-ion batteries
in electric vehicles using machine learning algorithms like
KNN, SVR, DT, and RF, based on direct battery measurements
(voltage, current, temperature). The study proposes collabo-
ration with hardware manufacturers for better battery health
monitoring systems.
The advent of deep learning introduced advanced mod-
els [10], such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks,
capable of capturing temporal dependencies and improving
anomaly detection in battery systems [6], [11]. However,
the development of robust deep learning methods hinges on
the availability of large-scale, publicly accessible datasets.
In response, recent advancements in EV battery research
have produced datasets tailored to various tasks, including
anomaly detection, capacity estimation, and remaining useful
life (RUL) prediction. For instance, datasets such as Sultan
et al.
[8] and HUST [12] focus on controlled experimental
conditions, while large-scale datasets like EVBattery [1] pro-
vide diverse real-world charging data. Additionally, specialized
datasets address manufacturing defects through CT scans [13]
or explore capacity estimation using voltage relaxation pro-
ﬁles [14].
Xiong et al. [15] propose a lithium-ion battery health
prognosis method using real-world BMS in electric vehi-
cles. The approach combines partial charge voltage curves as
health indicators with a moving-window-based RUL prediction
model. While the method is well-suited for many applica-
tions, its reliance on linear degradation models may present
challenges when applied to batteries exhibiting complex degra-
dation patterns.

AMARA KORBA et al.: SMTFL FOR BATTERY HEALTH AND CAPACITY ESTIMATION IN EVs
3
Deng et al. [16] propose a rapid health estimation frame-

work for in-service EV battery packs that combines a
digital-twin model based on an equivalent-circuit represen-
tation, feature extraction from short charging segments, and
deep convolutional neural networks with transfer learning
and domain adaptation to cope with limited labeled ﬁeld
data. Han et al. [17] emphasize the signiﬁcance of dynami-
cally reconﬁgurable battery management systems (RBSs) for
enhancing fault tolerance, improving charge and temperature
balancing, and achieving greater energy efﬁciency and opera-
tional ﬂexibility. While the proposed approach offers valuable
advancements, the implementation of RBSs may encounter
challenges such as the computational demands of optimization
algorithms, increased hardware design requirements, and prac-
tical considerations like managing transient behaviors during
switch operations.
Liu et al. [18] tackle the challenge of battery state of health

(SoH) estimation under limited sample conditions by intro-
ducing a reﬁned composite multiscale discrete sine entropy
(RCMDSE) algorithm. Similarly, Kumari et al. [19] propose
a hybrid approach for estimating state of charge, health,
and temperature (SoC, SoH, SoT). Their method combines
an emperor penguin-based residual network-110 (R110) with
bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) networks.
This approach demonstrates signiﬁcant promise, achieving
high accuracy on EV drive cycles simulated in MATLAB.
However, the reliance on advanced optimization techniques,
such as simulated annealing, may limit its real-time applica-
bility in resource-constrained environments. Kant et al., [20]
proposed a method that integrates a bidirectional recurrent
neural network and long-short-term memory (biRNN-LSTM)
to improve the prediction of the state of health (SoH) by
identifying complex patterns and improving accuracy.
Despite notable advancements in battery diagnostics and

capacity estimation, several limitations persist within the
state of the art. Approaches targeting complex degrada-
tion behaviors often fail to capture nonlinear dynamics [8],
while recent innovations [17], [19] face challenges related
to computational overhead, limiting real-time applicability
in resource-constrained EV. Many methods rely on datasets
generated under controlled laboratory conditions [6], [11],
restricting their generalizability to diverse real-world sce-
narios. Moreover, existing techniques often assume that EV
data can be centrally collected, overlooking critical privacy
concerns.
Federated learning (FL) has recently gained traction as

a distributed training paradigm in a variety of application
domains. For instance, Wu et al. [21] employ federated deep
reinforcement learning to perform multi-objective optimization
in STAR-RIS-aided satellite–aerial–ground integrated net-
works (SAGINs). In the context of battery health monitoring
and state-of-health (SoH) estimation, several studies [22],
[23], [24] have leveraged FL-based designs. Abbaraju and
Kundu [22] propose a federated ensemble learning (FEL)
approach that combines federated learning and ensemble learn-
ing to enhance SoH estimation. Their solution relies on an
LSTM model that is updated after each trip, leveraging het-
erogeneous data sources such as trafﬁc conditions and weather.

Wang et al. [23] introduce an adaptive multi-personalized fed-
erated learning (AMFL) algorithm that reﬁnes SoH estimation
by dynamically adjusting local models through personalized
layers and client clustering while incorporating a differential
privacy mechanism. Similarly, Wong et al. [24] develop a
decentralized federated learning approach for Li-ion battery
SoH forecasting, featuring an improved client selection strat-
egy and real-world validation experiments.
Despite notable progress, existing battery diagnostic meth-

ods exhibit several limitations. Model-based approaches often
rely on simpliﬁed linear degradation assumptions [15], failing
to capture complex real-world aging dynamics. Federated
learning (FL) methods for SoH estimation [22], [23], [24]
reduce data centralization but impose signiﬁcant computational
burdens on resource-constrained EVs and lack energy-efﬁcient
training schedules, which could impact battery autonomy.
Moreover, they typically focus on a single task (e.g., SoH
estimation), requiring separate models for different diagnostics
and increasing system complexity. Many methods are also
evaluated on controlled laboratory datasets [6], [11], limiting
their applicability to diverse real-world conditions.
To address these gaps, we propose a Split Multi-Task

Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework that: (1) employs
a Transformer-based encoder to model nonlinear temporal
dependencies; (2) reduces on-device computation by ofﬂoad-
ing heavy layers to edge infrastructure via split learning,
where only early layers are trained locally; (3) incorporates
differential privacy mechanisms to protect sensitive battery
data during model updates; (4) uniﬁes battery health anomaly
detection and capacity estimation into a single model, eliminat-
ing the need for separate, task-speciﬁc models and optimizing
parameter efﬁciency; (5) schedules training exclusively during
charging sessions to preserve EV battery life; and (6) is
validated on the large-scale real-world EVBattery dataset [1]
to ensure practical relevance. This innovative framework
effectively balances scalability, privacy preservation, and com-
putational efﬁciency, addressing the key challenges identiﬁed
in the state of the art.
Our framework integrates split learning and federated

architectures for battery health monitoring, balancing local
computation with global performance while incorporating
differential privacy. The following sections detail the archi-
tectural components, including the split Transformer model,
privacy-preserving training protocol, and federated coordina-
tion strategy.
The proposed system employs a hierarchical federated

learning architecture that integrates three primary components:
electric vehicles (EVs) as clients, edge servers deployed at
charging stations, and a global parameter server in the cloud.
The workﬂow is designed to ensure synchronization, prevent
version conﬂicts, and facilitate efﬁcient and scalable model
training. Figure 1 illustrates the interactions and hierarchical
structure among these components. At the start of each global

4
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON CONSUMER ELECTRONICS
aggregation where edge servers aggregate local updates from multiple EVs, and a cloud server aggregates edge updates for global model reﬁnement.

round, the cloud server distributes the global model to edge
servers located within charging stations, which then propagate
it to connected EVs. Each edge server collects model updates
from EVs during a station-level Aggregation Time Window
(ATW), performs local aggregation, and forwards the result
to the cloud server. The cloud operates within a longer
Synchronization Window (SW) to gather updates from all edge
servers, execute global aggregation, and redistribute the reﬁned
model.
The SMTFL framework leverages Power Line Communi-

cation (PLC) over the charging cable, standardized in ISO
15118 [25], to transmit model updates and intermediate rep-
resentations (smashed data) between EVs and edge servers.
This approach eliminates separate communication hardware,
reduces system complexity, and enhances security by utilizing
the naturally isolated channel of the charging cable. The
physical connection serves a dual purpose: power transfer and
data exchange. Communication is secured with mutual Trans-
port Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 [26], ensuring conﬁdentiality,
integrity, and authenticity. Charging stations communicate
with the cloud server via standard Internet connections (e.g.,
ﬁber, 4G/5G), enabling reliable transmission of aggregated
updates and global model distribution.
1) EV Participation in FL Rounds: To accurately estimate

the number of EVs connected to a charging station during
a given Aggregation Time Window (ATW), we propose a
mathematical model incorporating key variables: the arrival
rate of EVs (λEV ), the average session duration (Tsession),

and the station’s capacity (Nmax). The goal is to determine
the number of EVs utilizing the station within the ATW
while accounting for constraints such as the limited number
of charging points and varying levels of station utilization.
The arrival of EVs at a charging station is modeled as a

Poisson process with average arrival rate λEV (EVs per unit
time). During an ATW of duration TAT W, the total expected
arrivals is Narrivals = λEV · TAT W. The actual number of
EVs simultaneously connected during the ATW is inﬂuenced
by Tsession, Nmax, and an occupation factor ρ (fraction of
charging points typically in use):

In practice, EVs may not complete local training or transmit

AMARA KORBA et al.: SMTFL FOR BATTERY HEALTH AND CAPACITY ESTIMATION IN EVs
5

The subsequent SW at the cloud level provides additional
buffering, allowing edge servers to forward aggregated models
without requiring strict synchronization. Moreover, if an EV
disconnects prematurely, it can resume training in a later
session by downloading the latest global model. This design
ensures robust operation under realistic, asynchronous update
patterns and connectivity variations, making the system prac-
tical for real-world deployment.
2) EV-Level Operations: When an EV connects to a charg-

ing station, it downloads the client-side portion (ﬁrst two
Transformer layers) of the global model. Using local bat-
tery data, the EV performs forward and backward passes in
coordination with the edge server to update its local lay-
ers. Throughout this process, differential privacy mechanisms
are applied to both activations and weight updates. After
completing local training, the EV transmits its updated and
privacy-preserving client-side weights to the edge server for
aggregation.

3) Edge-Level
Operations:
Each
charging
station
is

equipped with an edge server that coordinates local training
and performs intermediate aggregation. Operating within a
ﬁxed Aggregation Time Window (ATW), the edge server
collects and aggregates client-side weight updates from con-
nected EVs. If no EVs connect during an ATW, aggregation
is skipped to conserve resources. The edge server also trains
the server-side layers using smashed data received from EVs.
Once the ATW ends, the edge server transmits the locally
updated model (aggregated client-side weights and updated
server-side layers) to the global server during the Synchro-
nization Window (SW).
4) Cloud-Level Operations: At the cloud level, the server

acts as a global parameter server, operating within a longer SW
to ensure all edge servers have sufﬁcient time to transmit their
aggregated models. The cloud server collects and integrates
model updates from all active edge servers, performs global
aggregation, and then redistributes the updated global model
back to the charging stations. Stations subsequently provide
the updated model to EVs upon their next connections, closing
the federated learning loop.
The prediction model employs a Transformer encoder to

process multivariate time-series data, performing two critical
tasks in parallel: battery health anomaly detection (binary
classiﬁcation)
and
capacity
estimation
(regression).
The

Transformer encoder is selected for its superior ability to
capture long-range temporal dependencies, which are essential
for accurate battery diagnostics. The model comprises six
encoder layers, each containing a multi-head self-attention
mechanism and a feed-forward network. In our split learning
conﬁguration,
the
architecture
is
divided

Given the sensitivity of battery operational data, this section
establishes our comprehensive security framework.
1) Threat Model: Our framework considers two primary
adversary classes:
• External Network Adversaries: Third parties capable

of intercepting communications between EVs and edge
servers, including potential PLC channel eavesdropping
despite physical isolation.
• Honest-but-Curious Edge Servers: Edge servers that

follow the protocol but attempt to infer sensitive infor-
mation. These adversaries could leverage split learning
vulnerabilities, such as analyzing smashed data to recon-
struct raw inputs or infer properties of the training data.

In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed

framework using the EVBattery dataset [1]. We ﬁrst introduce
the dataset and experimental setup, then present performance
under constant and dynamic participation scenarios for both
tasks. Subsequently, we provide a detailed complexity anal-
ysis of our framework. Finally, we compare and discuss our
approach against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.
We evaluate our framework using the EVBattery dataset [1],

a large-scale real-world benchmark for EV battery diagnos-
tics. The dataset comprises charging snippets collected under
diverse conditions—including fast/slow charging and varying
temperatures—from three anonymized manufacturers. Each
record contains 128-step time-series of eight features (voltage,
current, temperature, SOC, etc.) and meta-information (vehicle
ID, mileage, snippet index). Binary health labels (0: normal,
1: anomaly) and continuous capacity labels (28.28–46.23 Ah)
accompany each sample. A full description is given in Table I;
additional dataset speciﬁcs are available in the original publi-
cation [1].
The dataset was prepared from raw .pkl ﬁles containing

multivariate time-series data and metadata. Sequences were
converted into NumPy arrays, and entries with missing or
invalid values were discarded. Valid capacity labels (non-zero)
were retained as regression targets, while anomaly labels were
encoded as binary values (0: normal, 1: anomalies such as
lithium plating or thermal runaway). For normalization, all
time-series features were standardized per feature (zero mean,
unit variance) using a StandardScaler ﬁtted exclusively
on the training set. Capacity labels were similarly normalized.

The input data is projected into a 64-dimensional embed-

data distributions vary across clients, we implement a label-

Non-Identically Distributed) experiments. Each EV client is
assigned a dominant class (class 0, normal samples) while
ensuring a minimum of 3× batch size samples from the
minority class (class 1, anomalies). This approach creates
heterogeneous local data distributions, reﬂecting real-world
conditions where certain EV clients may observe more
frequent anomalies than others. Table III presents the result-

run, clearly showing the label-skew while maintaining the
minimum-sample constraint for both classes.
We validate our evaluation using 5-fold cross-validation.

To ensure robust assessment, the folds are constructed with a
strict temporal order: within each fold, the training data strictly
precedes the test data in time, eliminating temporal data
leakage. Additionally, we ensure that no EV client (identiﬁed
by unique vehicle IDs) is shared between the training and
test sets of any fold, preventing cross-client leakage and
guaranteeing complete isolation between model development
and evaluation data.

1) Computational Complexity: To evaluate the computa-

tional complexity of our SMTFL framework, we calculate the
Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) required for training both
the client-side and server-side models.
The client-side model has Pclient = 67,520 parameters

(embedding: 576 + 2 transformer layers: 2 × 33,472 =
66,944). The server-side model has Pserver = 134,018 param-
eters (4 transformer layers: 4 × 33,472 = 133,888+ classiﬁ-
cation head: 65+ regression head: 65). Each transformer layer
consists of multi-head attention (16,640 parameters), feed-
forward network (16,576), and two LayerNorm layers (256).
The self-attention mechanism, which dominates computa-

tional cost, has quadratic complexity with respect to sequence
length L. For each transformer layer, the dominant FLOPs per
sample per epoch come from computing the query-key product
and the attention-weighted value aggregation, each requiring
approximately 2L2d operations per forward pass. Accounting
for both forward and backward passes, the total FLOPs per
sample per layer is approximately 12L2d.

across the Non-IID distribution shown in Table III), and E =

- Server side (4 transformer layers):
FLOPsserver ≈4×12L2d×Nsamples × E =3.86 × 1011 FLOPs.

energy consumption makes the framework particularly suitable
for resource-constrained EVs during charging sessions.
2) Communication and Energy Overhead: Our framework

leverages Power Line Communication (PLC) during charg-
ing sessions, utilizing the existing power line infrastructure
without requiring additional network resources and eliminating
separate wireless transmission energy costs. The communica-
tion load per training round consists of uploading intermediate
activations (smashed data) and downloading gradients, each
approximately 1 MB per batch (B = 32, T = 128, dmodel =
64), plus 0.4 MB for client-side model updates, totaling ∼2.4
MB per round. Over 20 rounds (achieving 96% accuracy
and 0.43 MAE), an EV exchanges about 48 MB, orders of
magnitude less than transmitting raw battery time-series data
(∼100 MB). Energy overhead is supplied by the grid; with an
embedded GPU (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, 30 W peak)
and ∼10 s per round, each round consumes 0.083 Wh. A 20-
round session thus uses 1.66 Wh, which is less than 0.02% of
a typical fast-charging session (10 kWh). Consequently, the
framework introduces negligible communication and energy
overhead while preserving the EV’s primary function.

This paper introduced a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning

(SMTFL) framework for joint battery health anomaly detec-
tion and capacity estimation in electric vehicles (EVs). The
proposed approach combines a Transformer-based encoder
with a split federated architecture to achieve state-of-the-art
performance while addressing critical challenges in scala-
bility, privacy, and energy efﬁciency. Experimental results
demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods,
achieving an accuracy of 98.9% for anomaly detection and a
MAE of 0.32 for capacity estimation. These results validate the
model’s capability to capture complex temporal dependencies
and feature interactions across both tasks. By enabling EVs to
train a single uniﬁed model locally and ofﬂoading heavy com-
putations to edge servers, the SMTFL framework signiﬁcantly
reduces on-device resource requirements. Moreover, privacy
is preserved through differential privacy mechanisms and split

learning, while training is scheduled exclusively during charg-
ing sessions to minimize energy overhead. Collectively, these
attributes make the SMTFL framework a practical and efﬁcient
solution for large-scale, privacy-aware EV battery diagnos-
tics. Future work will focus on extending the framework to
additional battery management system (BMS) tasks, such as
predicting battery lifespan and identifying speciﬁc component
failures. We also plan to explore adaptive split points that
dynamically adjust the computation ofﬂoading based on device
capabilities and network conditions, as well as design more
sophisticated multitask models that integrate a broader set of
BMS functions without compromising efﬁciency.

RELATED WORK

Battery diagnostics and capacity estimation are critical research areas for ensuring the safety, reliability, and operational efﬁciency of electric vehicles (EVs). Early approaches often relied on statistical models and traditional machine learning techniques, such as statistical distribution analysis and canonical algorithms, to diagnose faults and detect anomalies [5], [6]. More recently, Li et al. [7] review artiﬁcial neural network (ANN) approaches for state-of-health (SoH) estimation and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, discussing battery aging mechanisms, available datasets, and ANN architectures, and outlining key challenges related to deployment feasibility and model interpretability. Sultan et al. [8] propose an active cell balancing system to address imbalanced state of charge (SoC) in EV lithium-ion battery packs caused by cell inconsistencies. The study evaluates seven machine learning models for predicting battery lifespan and remaining useful life (RUL). Das et al. [9] estimate the state of health (SoH) of lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles using machine learning algorithms like KNN, SVR, DT, and RF, based on direct battery measurements (voltage, current, temperature). The study proposes collaboration with hardware manufacturers for better battery health monitoring systems. The advent of deep learning introduced advanced models [10], such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, capable of capturing temporal dependencies and improving anomaly detection in battery systems [6], [11]. However, the development of robust deep learning methods hinges on the availability of large-scale, publicly accessible datasets. In response, recent advancements in EV battery research have produced datasets tailored to various tasks, including anomaly detection, capacity estimation, and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction. For instance, datasets such as Sultan et al. [8] and HUST [12] focus on controlled experimental conditions, while large-scale datasets like EVBattery [1] provide diverse real-world charging data. Additionally, specialized datasets address manufacturing defects through CT scans [13] or explore capacity estimation using voltage relaxation pro- ﬁles [14]. Xiong et al. [15] propose a lithium-ion battery health prognosis method using real-world BMS in electric vehicles. The approach combines partial charge voltage curves as health indicators with a moving-window-based RUL prediction model. While the method is well-suited for many applications, its reliance on linear degradation models may present challenges when applied to batteries exhibiting complex degradation patterns.
AMARA KORBA et al.: SMTFL FOR BATTERY HEALTH AND CAPACITY ESTIMATION IN EVs 3

Deng et al. [16] propose a rapid health estimation framework for in-service EV battery packs that combines a digital-twin model based on an equivalent-circuit representation, feature extraction from short charging segments, and deep convolutional neural networks with transfer learning and domain adaptation to cope with limited labeled ﬁeld data. Han et al. [17] emphasize the signiﬁcance of dynamically reconﬁgurable battery management systems (RBSs) for enhancing fault tolerance, improving charge and temperature balancing, and achieving greater energy efﬁciency and operational ﬂexibility. While the proposed approach offers valuable advancements, the implementation of RBSs may encounter challenges such as the computational demands of optimization algorithms, increased hardware design requirements, and practical considerations like managing transient behaviors during switch operations.

Liu et al. [18] tackle the challenge of battery state of health (SoH) estimation under limited sample conditions by introducing a reﬁned composite multiscale discrete sine entropy (RCMDSE) algorithm. Similarly, Kumari et al. [19] propose a hybrid approach for estimating state of charge, health, and temperature (SoC, SoH, SoT). Their method combines an emperor penguin-based residual network-110 (R110) with bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) networks. This approach demonstrates signiﬁcant promise, achieving high accuracy on EV drive cycles simulated in MATLAB. However, the reliance on advanced optimization techniques, such as simulated annealing, may limit its real-time applicability in resource-constrained environments. Kant et al., [20] proposed a method that integrates a bidirectional recurrent neural network and long-short-term memory (biRNN-LSTM) to improve the prediction of the state of health (SoH) by identifying complex patterns and improving accuracy.

Despite notable advancements in battery diagnostics andcapacity estimation, several limitations persist within the state of the art. Approaches targeting complex degradation behaviors often fail to capture nonlinear dynamics [8], while recent innovations [17], [19] face challenges related to computational overhead, limiting real-time applicability in resource-constrained EV. Many methods rely on datasets generated under controlled laboratory conditions [6], [11], restricting their generalizability to diverse real-world scenarios. Moreover, existing techniques often assume that EV data can be centrally collected, overlooking critical privacy concerns.

Federated learning (FL) has recently gained traction asa distributed training paradigm in a variety of application domains. For instance, Wu et al. [21] employ federated deep reinforcement learning to perform multi-objective optimization in STAR-RIS-aided satellite–aerial–ground integrated networks (SAGINs). In the context of battery health monitoring and state-of-health (SoH) estimation, several studies [22], [23], [24] have leveraged FL-based designs. Abbaraju and Kundu [22] propose a federated ensemble learning (FEL) approach that combines federated learning and ensemble learning to enhance SoH estimation. Their solution relies on an LSTM model that is updated after each trip, leveraging heterogeneous data sources such as trafﬁc conditions and weather.

Wang et al. [23] introduce an adaptive multi-personalized federated learning (AMFL) algorithm that reﬁnes SoH estimation by dynamically adjusting local models through personalized layers and client clustering while incorporating a differential privacy mechanism. Similarly, Wong et al. [24] develop a decentralized federated learning approach for Li-ion battery SoH forecasting, featuring an improved client selection strategy and real-world validation experiments.

Despite notable progress, existing battery diagnostic methods exhibit several limitations. Model-based approaches often rely on simpliﬁed linear degradation assumptions [15], failing to capture complex real-world aging dynamics. Federated learning (FL) methods for SoH estimation [22], [23], [24] reduce data centralization but impose signiﬁcant computational burdens on resource-constrained EVs and lack energy-efﬁcient training schedules, which could impact battery autonomy. Moreover, they typically focus on a single task (e.g., SoH estimation), requiring separate models for different diagnostics and increasing system complexity. Many methods are also evaluated on controlled laboratory datasets [6], [11], limiting their applicability to diverse real-world conditions.

To address these gaps, we propose a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework that: (1) employs a Transformer-based encoder to model nonlinear temporal dependencies; (2) reduces on-device computation by ofﬂoading heavy layers to edge infrastructure via split learning, where only early layers are trained locally; (3) incorporates differential privacy mechanisms to protect sensitive battery data during model updates; (4) uniﬁes battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation into a single model, eliminating the need for separate, task-speciﬁc models and optimizing parameter efﬁciency; (5) schedules training exclusively during charging sessions to preserve EV battery life; and (6) is validated on the large-scale real-world EVBattery dataset [1] to ensure practical relevance. This innovative framework effectively balances scalability, privacy preservation, and computational efﬁciency, addressing the key challenges identiﬁed in the state of the art.

SMTFL FRAMEWORK

Our framework integrates split learning and federatedarchitectures for battery health monitoring, balancing local computation with global performance while incorporating differential privacy. The following sections detail the architectural components, including the split Transformer model, privacy-preserving training protocol, and federated coordination strategy.
System Model

The proposed system employs a hierarchical federatedlearning architecture that integrates three primary components: electric vehicles (EVs) as clients, edge servers deployed at charging stations, and a global parameter server in the cloud. The workﬂow is designed to ensure synchronization, prevent version conﬂicts, and facilitate efﬁcient and scalable model training. Figure 1 illustrates the interactions and hierarchical structure among these components. At the start of each global

EV-Level Operations: When an EV connects to a charging station, it downloads the client-side portion (ﬁrst two Transformer layers) of the global model. Using local bat- tery data, the EV performs forward and backward passes in coordination with the edge server to update its local lay- ers. Throughout this process, differential privacy mechanisms are applied to both activations and weight updates. After completing local training, the EV transmits its updated and privacy-preserving client-side weights to the edge server for aggregation. Edge-Level Operations: Each charging station is equipped with an edge server that coordinates local training and performs intermediate aggregation. Operating within a ﬁxed Aggregation Time Window (ATW), the edge server collects and aggregates client-side weight updates from con- nected EVs. If no EVs connect during an ATW, aggregation is skipped to conserve resources. The edge server also trains the server-side layers using smashed data received from EVs. Once the ATW ends, the edge server transmits the locally updated model (aggregated client-side weights and updated server-side layers) to the global server during the Synchro- nization Window (SW). Cloud-Level Operations: At the cloud level, the server acts as a global parameter server, operating within a longer SW to ensure all edge servers have sufﬁcient time to transmit their aggregated models. The cloud server collects and integrates model updates from all active edge servers, performs global aggregation, and then redistributes the updated global model back to the charging stations. Stations subsequently provide the updated model to EVs upon their next connections, closing the federated learning loop.

Prediction Model Architecture

The prediction model employs a Transformer encoder toprocess multivariate time-series data, performing two critical tasks in parallel: battery health anomaly detection (binary classiﬁcation) and capacity estimation (regression). The Transformer encoder is selected for its superior ability to capture long-range temporal dependencies, which are essential for accurate battery diagnostics. The model comprises six encoder layers, each containing a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network. In our split learning conﬁguration, the architecture is divided at a preciseboundary: the ﬁrst two encoder layers form the client-side (EV) component, while the remaining four layers, along with global pooling and task-speciﬁc heads, constitute the server-side (edge) component. This split follows established privacy–complexity trade-offs in split learning [27]: early layers extract low-level features with minimal privacy risk, while deeper, computationally intensive layers are ofﬂoadedto the edge server. During operation, the EV processes raw data through the ﬁrst two layers, producing intermediate activations (smashed data) of dimension [batch_size, sequence_length=128, d_model=64], which aretransmitted to the edge server.

Split Federated Training

The client-side model processes raw battery data locally, transforming it into intermediate representations (smashed data). To preserve privacy, Gaussian noise is added to the smashed data before transmission, ensuring differential privacy. The noisy smashed data are then sent to the edge server, which completes the forward pass using its layers, computes the multi-task loss, and backpropagates gradients through its own layers and back to the smashed data. These gradients are returned to the EV, which uses them to update its local layers via backpropagation. After completing a ﬁxed number of local epochs, the EV uploads its updated client-side weights, again applying differential privacy by adding Gaussian noise, to the edge server for aggregation. This design reduces the computational load on EVs while safeguarding data privacy and ensuring scalable, distributed training.

PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of the proposedframework using the EVBattery dataset [1]. We ﬁrst introduce the dataset and experimental setup, then present performance under constant and dynamic participation scenarios for both tasks. Subsequently, we provide a detailed complexity analysis of our framework. Finally, we compare and discuss our approach against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.
EVBattery Dataset

We evaluate our framework using the EVBattery dataset [1], a large-scale real-world benchmark for EV battery diagnostics. The dataset comprises charging snippets collected under diverse conditions—including fast/slow charging and varying temperatures—from three anonymized manufacturers. Each record contains 128-step time-series of eight features (voltage, current, temperature, SOC, etc.) and meta-information (vehicle ID, mileage, snippet index). Binary health labels (0: normal, 1: anomaly) and continuous capacity labels (28.28–46.23 Ah) accompany each sample. A full description is given in Table I; additional dataset speciﬁcs are available in the original publication [1].

The cleaned dataset contained no missing values. To preserve real-world conditions, the natural class imbalance was maintained for anomaly detection; in Non-IID splits, each client was guaranteed at least three-batch-size samples per class to prevent extreme skew, without any synthetic resampling. This approach ensures a realistic evaluation of the model under practical data distributions.

The dataset was prepared from raw .pkl ﬁles containingmultivariate time-series data and metadata. Sequences were converted into NumPy arrays, and entries with missing or invalid values were discarded. Valid capacity labels (non-zero) were retained as regression targets, while anomaly labels were encoded as binary values (0: normal, 1: anomalies such as lithium plating or thermal runaway). For normalization, all time-series features were standardized per feature (zero mean, unit variance) using a StandardScaler ﬁtted exclusively on the training set. Capacity labels were similarly normalized.

The architectural details and hyperparameters of the Transformer model are summarized in Table II. The model was

implemented in Python 3.9 using the PyTorch 2.0 deep learning framework. It comprises a stack of six encoder layers, each consisting of an 8-head self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network with 128-dimensional hidden states. The input data is projected into a 64-dimensional embedding space and enriched with sinusoidal positional encodings to retain temporal information. The loss function combines binary cross-entropy for anomaly detection and mean squared error for capacity estimation to ensure effective training across tasks. For privacy protection, Gaussian differential privacy was applied with noise scale

Communication and Energy Overhead: Our framework leverages Power Line Communication (PLC) during charg- ing sessions, utilizing the existing power line infrastructure without requiring additional network resources and eliminating separate wireless transmission energy costs. The communica- tion load per training round consists of uploading intermediate activations (smashed data) and downloading gradients, each approximately 1 MB per batch (B = 32, T = 128, dmodel = 64), plus 0.4 MB for client-side model updates, totaling ∼2.4 MB per round. Over 20 rounds (achieving 96% accuracy and 0.43 MAE), an EV exchanges about 48 MB, orders of magnitude less than transmitting raw battery time-series data (∼100 MB). Energy overhead is supplied by the grid; with an embedded GPU (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, 30 W peak) and ∼10 s per round, each round consumes 0.083 Wh. A 20- round session thus uses 1.66 Wh, which is less than 0.02% of a typical fast-charging session (10 kWh). Consequently, the framework introduces negligible communication and energy overhead while preserving the EV’s primary function.

Comparative Analysis

We evaluate our framework against both centralized andfederated baselines to contextualize its performance. Although battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation have been studied in the literature, to the best of our knowledge, only [1] utilized the EVBattery dataset, enabling a direct comparison. Notably, the authors of [1] employed multiple machine learning methods, providing a valuable opportunity to benchmark our solution against various approaches. However, their work did not incorporate federated learning (FL). Therefore, we implemented FL-based baselines (LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU) to compare our solution against FL methods as well. Figure 5 illustrates the performance comparison of our solution with centralized ML models from [1] for both tasks: AUROC for Task 1 (battery health anomaly detection) and RMSE for Task 2 (battery capacity estimation). These metrics were not selected arbitrarily but were adopted because [1] exclusively relied on them, ensuring a consistent and meaningful comparison.

The AUROC scores demonstrate a clear improvementachieved by the proposed models (MTFL and SMTFL). While traditional methods such as AE, Deep SVDD, and LSTMAD exhibit moderate performance, our models signiﬁcantly outperform them, reaching an AUROC of 99.9%, marking a

substantial advancement in battery health anomaly detection. For the capacity estimation task, evaluated through RMSE, the proposed models also show superior performance. Baseline methods such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and GCNN achieve RMSE values ranging from 1.39 to 1.42, indicating limitations in accurately predicting capacity under complex conditions. In contrast, the proposed models achieve RMSE values of 0.64 and 0.66, respectively, signiﬁcantly reducing the prediction error. The strong performance of SMTFL can be attributed to its ability to effectively capture multivariate temporal dependencies and feature interactions, leveraging the advanced Transformer-based architecture integrated into the federated learning framework.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This paper introduced a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework for joint battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation in electric vehicles (EVs). The proposed approach combines a Transformer-based encoder with a split federated architecture to achieve state-of-the-art performance while addressing critical challenges in scalability, privacy, and energy efﬁciency. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 98.9% for anomaly detection and a MAE of 0.32 for capacity estimation. These results validate the model’s capability to capture complex temporal dependencies and feature interactions across both tasks. By enabling EVs to train a single uniﬁed model locally and ofﬂoading heavy computations to edge servers, the SMTFL framework signiﬁcantly reduces on-device resource requirements. Moreover, privacy is preserved through differential privacy mechanisms and split

learning, while training is scheduled exclusively during charging sessions to minimize energy overhead. Collectively, these attributes make the SMTFL framework a practical and efﬁcient solution for large-scale, privacy-aware EV battery diagnostics. Future work will focus on extending the framework to additional battery management system (BMS) tasks, such as predicting battery lifespan and identifying speciﬁc component failures. We also plan to explore adaptive split points that dynamically adjust the computation ofﬂoading based on device capabilities and network conditions, as well as design more sophisticated multitask models that integrate a broader set of BMS functions without compromising efﬁciency.

By enabling EVs to train a single uniﬁed model locally and ofﬂoading heavy computations to edge servers, the SMTFL framework signiﬁcantly reduces on-device resource requirements. Moreover, privacy is preserved through differential privacy mechanisms and split

Batteries, as the cornerstone of EV performance, are susceptible to capacity degradation, thermal instability, and anomalies that compromise efﬁciency and safety. Traditional diagnostic approaches, relying on physics-based models and heuristic thresholds, often fail to address the complexity and variability of real-world EV operations, necessitating scalable, efﬁcient, and privacy-preserving solutions. This paper presents a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework that leverages a Transformer-based architecture to address the dual challenges of battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation. By combining the efﬁciency of split learning with the collaborative beneﬁts of federated learning, the proposed system enables EVs to train and share partial model updates while retaining sensitive data locally. Experimental results on a recent large-scale EV dataset demonstrate the superior performance of the SMTFL framework, achieving an accuracy of 98.9% for battery health anomaly detection and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.32 Ah for capacity estimation, corresponding to a relative error of approximately 1.80%, signiﬁcantly outperforming state-of-the-art approaches. By training a single model for both tasks and performing computations during charging sessions, the framework minimizes energy consumption and computational overhead, ensuring practicality for large-scale deployment in real-world EV systems.

In this work, we distinguish between battery health anomalydetection and capacity estimation, two related yet distinct diagnostic tasks. Following established battery diagnostics conventions [1], State of Health (SoH) refers to the overall degradation of the battery (often expressed as a percentage of initial capacity), whereas capacity estimation quantiﬁes the absolute remaining charge in ampere-hours (Ah). Accordingly, we frame health monitoring as a binary anomaly detection task (normal vs. anomalous conditions such as lithium plating or thermal runaway), and capacity estimation as a regression task.

The complexity of battery diagnostics stems from the highlyvariable operating environments of EVs [2], which involve ﬂuctuating charging and discharging cycles, environmental conditions, and aging effects. Traditional methods, such as physics-based models or predeﬁned threshold-based diagnostics, struggle to adapt to such real-world complexities, often leading to suboptimal performance. Moreover, the integration of EVs into connected vehicular networks introduces additional constraints, including the need for scalable solutions that can handle large data volumes while preserving data privacy.
